title: Sanctuary at Abu Sufyan's house
hookLine: entering Mecca, he declares safety for anyone in their own home, in the sacred mosque, or in Abu Sufyan's house
carry: whoever shuts his door is safe

cards: Mecca, the city that drove him out, is about to be entered by a large army, and the people inside are afraid of what it will do to them. Now, a name from two days ago: Abu Sufyan, the man who couldn't lie to the emperor.
The sirah tells that he has just come over to the Muslim side, and he rides back into Mecca ahead of the army with a message from the Prophet. He stands in front of his own people and shouts it.
Today: sanctuary at Abu Sufyan's house.

teach.b: The message is about safety. Sahih Muslim records the words of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe.
Whoever lays down his weapons is safe. Whoever shuts his door is safe. The sirah of Ibn Ishaq adds the sacred mosque around the Ka'bah as another place of safety.
Look at how wide that is. You don't have to change your religion to be covered. You don't have to come out and surrender in public.
You don't even have to leave your house. You only have to close your own front door, and you're protected.

teach.h: SAFETY COMES TO WHERE PEOPLE ARE.
teach.b: The safety comes to where people already are.
And look at whose house is named. Not the house of an old friend. The house of Abu Sufyan, who had led the Meccans against the Muslims.
Giving his home a share in the sanctuary is a kind of honor, and Abu Sufyan, of all people, is the one who announces it.

teach.h: WHOEVER SHUTS HIS DOOR IS SAFE.
teach.b: A man who had been an enemy is handed a way to protect his own city. In the story, people go indoors and into the mosque.

Muslims tell this as the day a city that had opposed him was entered with more mercy than it expected. Tomorrow: some of the people who had fought him hardest, and what happened when they came to him.

how: Muslims retell the entry into Mecca from Sahih Muslim and the sirah, and the declaration of safety for Abu Sufyan's house and for anyone behind a closed door is told as a picture of mercy at the moment of victory.

o: the Prophet's uncle who protected him in Mecca
the Meccan leader whose house became a sanctuary
the companion who hid with him in the cave

games.q: sanctuary at Abu Sufyan's house — tap the pairs.

s: only people who became Muslim were promised safety
anyone who shut their door, laid down weapons or entered Abu Sufyan's house was safe.
the house of a former enemy was named a sanctuary
Abu Sufyan had led the opposition; his house became a place of safety.
to be safe, people had to come out and surrender in public
they could simply stay inside and close the door.

games.q: you're in Mecca as the army arrives. you hear Abu Sufyan shouting. what does the message ask of you?
o: come out and surrender in the square.
shut your door and stay inside.
games.why: whoever shuts his door is safe. safety came to where people already were.

practice: Think of a person who may be a little afraid of you, a child after you've raised your voice, a coworker who made a mistake, someone you argued with, and notice what they might be bracing for.
Picture the smallest step that would tell them they're safe with you: a softer tone, a quick message, an easy word. If you pray, you can ask Allah to make you a place of safety for others.

wordCard.voice: Abu Sufyan. The Prophet declared his house itself a sanctuary when Mecca was entered, safe for anyone who stayed inside or laid down weapons. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'safe', the word repeated in each line of the declaration.

carryVoice: Your line: whoever shuts his door is safe. Safety came to where people already were. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the conquest of Mecca)
